# Letter of Aristeas Chapter 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Greek MS | **Section:** The Origin of the Septuagint — Ptolemy Commissions the LXX

---

**1** You've been eager to hear about our visit to Eleazar the Jewish High Priest and about matters of the law and divine affairs, Philocrates — so I've put together this detailed account for you.

**2** I know you're philosophically minded and that you think the greatest honor is to keep your mind free from materialism and to think seriously about what is genuinely good and true.

**3** Pursuing this kind of life is what has made me so devoted to these things — I'm drawn by my reverence for the beauty of virtue and the glory of people who actually live by it.

**4** Your existing detailed knowledge, combined with your commitment to philosophy, will help you follow this account.

**5** At the time when our father Philocrates was rewarded for his loyal service to the king — and when we ourselves were honored — I had the privilege of being present when the mission began.

**6** Demetrius of Phalerum was in charge of the royal library at the time. He had been given large amounts of money to collect — if possible — every book in the world.

**7** Through purchases and translations he assembled as many works as he could. When the king asked how many thousands of books he had, he replied: 'About two hundred thousand, your majesty — and I plan to bring the number to five hundred thousand before long.'

**8** He also mentioned that the books of Jewish law were still needed, among others, and that they were well worth copying and adding to the royal library.

**9** 'What's stopping you from writing to the High Priest in Jerusalem?' I asked. 'Ask him to send men of excellent character who can interpret the law. I could then produce faithful translations for the royal library.'

**10** Demetrius liked the idea and told the king. The king, when informed, ordered letters to be written to the High Priest requesting that seventy-two elders — six from each tribe — be sent to him.

**11** I knew you'd be glad to hear this, Philocrates. Before I begin the account, let me make the purpose of the whole undertaking clear: it was for the sake of the Jewish law.

**12** Since God is the ruler of all people — the same God who made us all and sustains the world and meets our needs — I decided to make a case for the Jewish captives.

**13** Those who had been unjustly taken from their homeland deserved to go home, and the king would gain great honor by ordering their release.

**14** I went to the king and made their case: 'Your majesty, the men brought here by force from Judea have served you and your father faithfully.'

**15** 'They are men of exceptional virtue and devotion. I ask you to grant them their freedom and to write to your governors throughout the kingdom allowing them to return home.'

**16** The king was very pleased and replied: 'It is right that those who have served loyally should receive their freedom. I will write to all the governors, tax collectors, and administrators throughout the kingdom.'

**17** The king issued a proclamation freeing all Jewish captives — men, women, and children — granting each their freedom.

**18** He also commanded that the royal treasury compensate every master for each person freed.

**19** The number freed was more than one hundred thousand.

**20** Besides these, soldiers who had been brought before your father's time and were still serving were also to be freed.

**21** I've included the full text of the decree here so its scope can be fully appreciated.

**22** The Decree reads: 'All who came into this land with our father Ptolemy, whether voluntarily or under compulsion for military service, or who were brought here during the subsequent troubles — all such persons are to receive their freedom.'

**23** 'Payment is to be made for each such person from the royal treasury, and their former masters are to be compensated at twenty drachmas per head.'

**24** 'I am convinced that freeing so many people will please the God of the universe — the very one who has kept our reign peaceful and supremely renowned throughout the world.'

**25** The officials reported the total cost to the king: one thousand four hundred and sixty talents.

**26** The king agreed immediately: 'Let it be done — for the sake of our dignity and the honor of God.'

**27** The captives were freed. Great rejoicing spread through the land, and the king was showered with blessings.

**28** Once this was done, Demetrius brought up the translation project again with the king: 'The next step is to send for the men from Jerusalem who will do the translation.'

**29** The king was pleased: 'Write to the High Priest Eleazar. Ask him to send six elders from each tribe — men of excellent character and broad learning — so we can understand the law and translate it properly.'

**30** Here is the full text of the letter that was sent.

**31** 'King Ptolemy to the High Priest Eleazar, greetings. It is our consistent policy to show kindness to all people, especially to those of outstanding character, and most especially to the people of your nation. We therefore wish to take this opportunity to demonstrate our goodwill to all your people.'

**32** 'We have released from our realm more than one hundred thousand Jewish captives. We paid their masters the appropriate sum and corrected whatever wrongs had been done.'

**33** 'Our purpose in doing this is to honor both you and God, whose law your people uphold.'

**34** 'We have decided to have your law translated into Greek. We believe it will be enormously beneficial for all people.'

**35** 'We ask you therefore to send six men from each of the twelve tribes — men of wisdom and learning who can produce an accurate translation of the law.'

**36** 'We believe this will greatly add to our reputation and that it will be a genuinely noble achievement.'

**37** 'We have also sent appropriate gifts for the temple from our own resources.'

**38** Eleazar read the letter and was very pleased. He said to the messengers: 'I will respond to the king without delay.'

**39** He chose seventy-two men, six from each tribe — men of outstanding character, extensive learning, and genuine piety.

**40** They were also deeply experienced in the law and fluent in Greek — it was essential that they be capable of rendering the Hebrew scriptures accurately into Greek.

**41** Their names were recorded. I will give the full list here so you can know exactly who these men were.

**42** From Reuben: Joseph, Ezekiah, Zachariah, John, Hezekiah, Elisha. From Simeon: Judas, Simon, Samuel, Adaeus, Mattathias, Eschlemias.

**43** From Levi: Theodosius, Jason, Jesus, Theodotus, Jonathan, Dositheus. From Judah: Caleb, Joseph, Simeon, Zachariah, Samuel, Selomias.

**44** And so on for the remaining tribes — six from each — until all seventy-two were chosen.

**45** They set out for Alexandria with Eleazar's letter, carrying with them the sacred scrolls of the law, written in golden letters on beautifully prepared parchment.

**46** When the king saw them he was very pleased and asked them many questions about the law and the wisdom of their people.

**47** He honored them greatly and held a magnificent feast in their honor, at which the wisest men of Egypt were also present.

**48** He asked the translators to answer one question per day throughout the feast.

**49** The king wanted to test their wisdom and their understanding of the law in this way.

**50** Everyone present was astonished by the quality of their answers, and the king himself declared he had never heard such wise replies.

**51** Before the translators arrived, the king had already prepared magnificent gifts to send to the temple in Jerusalem.

**52** Among the gifts was a great gold and silver table, encrusted with precious stones and of extraordinary craftsmanship.

**53** The craftsmen were the finest in all Egypt, and the king personally supervised the work, demanding the highest standards.

**54** The table was sized for the temple sanctuary and decorated with representations of every kind of fruit and flower.

**55** The border of the table had a vine pattern: pure gold tendrils, with clusters of grapes made from inlaid gems.

**56** At the corners were golden cups filled with incense, surrounded by wreaths of lilies and other flowers.

**57** The craftsmanship was unlike anything seen before. When it was finished the king inspected it and declared himself satisfied.

**58** He also had two large golden bowls made, carved with scenes depicting the history of the world from creation.

**59** These were intended for the temple's incense offerings and were filled with the finest incenses available.

**60** The king also sent golden vials and cups, along with large quantities of fine linen and purple cloth for the temple service.

**61** The king also sent pure golden incense burners and candelabra of the finest workmanship.

**62** Among them were thirty golden mixing bowls, twenty silver bowls, and goblets of fine crystal.

**63** The total value of the gifts was estimated at more than two hundred talents of gold.

**64** When the gifts were loaded onto the ships, the king himself came to the harbor to see them off.

**65** The king also sent a personal letter to Eleazar, expressing his desire for the translation to proceed.

**66** In the letter the king asked Eleazar to pray for him and for his kingdom.

**67** Eleazar received the gifts with great joy and gave thanks to God for inspiring the king.

**68** He sent back with the messengers his warmest greetings and a letter of his own.

**69** He wrote: 'King Ptolemy, beloved of God, to Eleazar the High Priest, greetings.'

**70** The High Priest praised the king's generosity and spoke of the benefits of the translation.

**71** He said that the work of translating the divine law was of the greatest importance.

**72** He promised that the seventy-two translators would work with all diligence and faithfulness.

**73** He assured the king that the men chosen were of the highest character and wisdom.

**74** He described the beauty and orderliness of the temple and the holy city.

**75** He told of the daily sacrifices offered for the king and his household.

**76** He gave the names of the seventy-two translators and their tribal affiliations.

**77** He concluded with a blessing: 'May God guard you and preserve your kingdom in peace.'

**78** The letter was received with joy at the royal court, and great preparations were made.

**79** The king ordered a magnificent reception to be prepared for the translators.

**80** The harbor was decorated, and food and gifts were prepared for their arrival.

**81** For seven days before their arrival the city was in festive preparation.

**82** And on the day they arrived, a great crowd came to the harbor to meet them.

**83** The city of Jerusalem is situated in the midst of a great hill, and the temple is at the highest point.

**84** The city is not large in extent, but it is built on the summit of a hill of considerable size.

**85** The temple faces east, and the morning sun illuminates it when it rises.

**86** There is a great outer court, and within it are the courts for the priests and the Levites.

**87** The sanctuary itself is divided into the holy place and the most holy place.

**88** No one enters the most holy place except the High Priest, and only on the Day of Atonement.

**89** The altar of burnt offering stands in the middle of the outer court, a great structure of stone.

**90** The priests perform their service in complete silence, and with the greatest reverence.

**91** There is a constant supply of wood for the altar fires, and the fires burn night and day.

**92** The water supply of the temple is remarkable — springs of pure water well up within the temple precincts.

**93** The whole building is constructed of massive stone blocks, fitted together without mortar.

**94** The skill of the builders was extraordinary, and the temple is a marvel of human craftsmanship.

**95** There are chambers around the outer court where the temple vessels are stored.

**96** The vessels of gold and silver are of extraordinary beauty and craftsmanship.

**97** Everything in the temple is arranged with the greatest order and beauty.

**98** The priests who serve in the temple are men of great dignity and holiness.

**99** They are dressed in white linen garments of the finest quality.

**100** Their service is conducted with perfect silence and order.

**101** The sight of the temple service is so majestic that it fills the beholder with awe.

**102** Eleazar the High Priest presides over all the temple service with great dignity.

**103** His vestments are of extraordinary beauty and covered with precious stones.

**104** On his head he wears the golden diadem with the sacred Name engraved upon it.

**105** His breastplate contains twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel.

**106** When the High Priest appears in his full vestments, he is a magnificent sight.

**107** The beauty of his appearance is beyond description, and all who see him stand in awe.

**108** The land surrounding Jerusalem is fertile and well-watered.

**109** The hills are covered with vines and olive trees and fig trees.

**110** The plains are rich in grain and produce of every kind.

**111** The people of the land are industrious and devoted to their God.

**112** Their laws govern every aspect of their lives, from the greatest matters to the smallest.

**113** They eat no food that has not been prepared according to their law.

**114** They observe the Sabbath with great strictness and do no work on that day.

**115** They observe the festivals of their law with joy and celebration.

**116** Their devotion to their law is the source of their strength as a people.

**117** They believe that the law was given to them by God himself through Moses.

**118** They regard the law as the greatest gift God has given to any people.

**119** Their wisdom comes from their constant study and practice of the law.

**120** All this I observed during my time in Jerusalem, and I was filled with admiration.

**121** Eleazar the High Priest is a man of great stature and beauty, and his bearing is dignified and noble.

**122** He welcomed us with great warmth and spoke to us about the law and the wisdom of God.

**123** He said: 'The law of God is the foundation of all wisdom, and those who live by it will know true happiness.'

**124** He spoke of the creation of the world and the wisdom with which God ordered it.

**125** He said: 'God made all things out of nothing, and he made them good, and he gave them to us to enjoy.'

**126** He spoke of the nature of God: 'God is one, and there is no other god besides him.'

**127** 'He is the creator of all things and the sustainer of all things, and he knows all things.'

**128** 'His wisdom is beyond all understanding, and his power is beyond all limitation.'

**129** He spoke of the law: 'Every commandment of the law has a reason and a purpose.'

**130** 'The laws about food teach us to control our desires and not to be enslaved by appetite.'

**131** 'The laws about the Sabbath teach us to honor God and to rest from our labors.'

**132** 'The laws about sacrifice teach us gratitude and devotion to God.'

**133** 'All the laws, taken together, teach us to live in a way that honors God and benefits our neighbors.'

**134** He spoke of justice: 'God requires us to deal justly with all people, without partiality.'

**135** 'We must not take advantage of the poor or the weak, but must defend their rights.'

**136** 'We must be honest in all our dealings and not deceive our neighbors in any way.'

**137** He spoke of the nature of true wisdom: 'Wisdom begins with the fear of God.'

**138** 'The wise man is not the one who has read many books, but the one who has learned to obey God.'

**139** 'True wisdom is shown in action, not in words.'

**140** He spoke of prayer: 'Prayer is not a matter of many words, but of a sincere heart.'

**141** 'God does not need our prayers, but we need to pray, for it disciplines our souls.'

**142** He spoke of the community: 'We are bound to one another as members of one body.'

**143** 'What harms one of us harms all of us, and what benefits one benefits all.'

**144** He spoke of hope: 'Those who suffer for God's sake will be rewarded.'

**145** 'The righteous may suffer in this life, but God will vindicate them in the end.'

**146** He spoke of death: 'Death is not the end, for the soul lives on after the body dies.'

**147** 'Those who have lived righteously will rest in peace, and those who have done evil will face judgment.'

**148** He spoke of the translation: 'It is a great thing that the king wishes to translate our law.'

**149** 'For the law of God is not only for the Jews, but for all people who seek wisdom.'

**150** 'All who read it and follow it will find the path to a good life.'

**151** He blessed the translators and prayed that God would guide their work.

**152** He said: 'May God open your minds to understand the depths of his law.'

**153** 'And may he guide your tongues to express his truth faithfully in another language.'

**154** He gave each of the seventy-two translators his personal blessing and a gift.

**155** The gifts were scrolls of the law, written by the finest scribes in Jerusalem.

**156** They were written on the finest parchment and in the most beautiful script.

**157** Eleazar also sent a letter with the translators to Ptolemy.

**158** The letter praised the king's wisdom and piety in undertaking the translation.

**159** It requested that when the translation was complete, the king treat it with the highest honor.

**160** It also requested that a copy be sent back to Jerusalem for the temple library.

**161** Eleazar said: 'May the God of Israel bless you and keep you, King Ptolemy.'

**162** 'May he prosper your kingdom and protect it from all enemies.'

**163** 'And may the translation of his law bring wisdom and blessing to all who read it.'

**164** We departed from Jerusalem with great joy and with a deep sense of the importance of our mission.

**165** The road back to Alexandria was long, but our hearts were light.

**166** We spoke much along the way of what we had seen and heard.

**167** We were all moved by the holiness and wisdom of Eleazar and the beauty of the temple.

**168** We were also moved by the devotion of the priests and the people to their law.

**169** I reflected much on what I had seen, and I was filled with a new respect for the Jewish people.

**170** Their devotion to their God and their law is something that puts many other peoples to shame.

**171** We arrived back in Alexandria filled with enthusiasm for the task ahead.

**172** The vestments of the High Priest are of extraordinary beauty and symbolic meaning.

**173** The breastplate contains twelve precious stones, one for each tribe of Israel.

**174** On the stones are engraved the names of the twelve patriarchs.

**175** The golden bells on the hem of the garment ring as the High Priest moves.

**176** The robe is of blue and purple and scarlet and fine twisted linen.

**177** On the hem are pomegranates of blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen.

**178** The ephod is of gold and blue and purple and scarlet and fine twisted linen.

**179** On the shoulder pieces are two stones of onyx, with the names of the twelve tribes engraved on them.

**180** The golden diadem on the High Priest's head bears the sacred Name.

**181** When the High Priest is dressed in his full vestments, he appears more than human.

**182** The splendor of his appearance inspires reverence in all who behold him.

**183** The garments are not merely beautiful — they are full of symbolic meaning.

**184** Each element of the vestments represents an aspect of the priestly calling.

**185** The High Priest wears these garments when he enters the sanctuary to make atonement.

**186** He represents before God all the people of Israel when he stands in the holy place.

**187** The king asked: 'How can a king be most powerful?' The scholar replied: 'By ruling himself first, and by doing justice to all. For the ruler who controls himself and deals justly will be honored by all his subjects.' The king was impressed.

**188** The king asked: 'What is the finest thing a king can do?' The scholar replied: 'To honor God and to do justice to all men, for these two things bring the greatest glory.' The king was impressed.

**189** The king asked: 'What is wisdom?' The scholar replied: 'Wisdom is knowing the things of God and of men, and applying that knowledge to the benefit of all.' The king was impressed.

**190** The king asked: 'What is strength?' The scholar replied: 'True strength is the mastery of oneself, for one who cannot govern himself cannot govern others.' The king was impressed.

**191** The king asked: 'What is the greatest honor a man can receive?' The scholar replied: 'The love of those over whom he rules, for this is a gift that cannot be bought.' The king was impressed.

**192** The king asked: 'How should a king treat his friends?' The scholar replied: 'As he would wish to be treated by them — with loyalty, honesty, and generosity.' The king was impressed.

**193** The king asked: 'What is the most important thing in life?' The scholar replied: 'To know God, for all other good things flow from that knowledge.' The king was impressed.

**194** The king asked: 'How should a king deal with enemies?' The scholar replied: 'With justice, not with cruelty. The wise king seeks to make friends of his enemies where possible.' The king was impressed.

**195** The king asked: 'What brings the most grief to a man?' The scholar replied: 'A guilty conscience, for it gives no rest by night or by day.' The king was impressed.

**196** The king asked: 'What brings the greatest happiness?' The scholar replied: 'Virtue, for it brings contentment that neither wealth nor power can give.' The king was impressed.

**197** The king asked: 'How should a king treat the poor?' The scholar replied: 'With the same justice as the rich, for God has made all men equal in soul.' The king was impressed.

**198** The king asked: 'What is the best preparation for a king before making a great decision?' The scholar replied: 'Prayer and reflection, for God gives wisdom to those who seek it with humility.' The king was impressed.

**199** The king asked: 'How should a man bear misfortune?' The scholar replied: 'With patience and trust in God, for all things are in his hands.' The king was impressed.

**200** The king asked: 'What is the nature of friendship?' The scholar replied: 'True friendship is built on virtue, and will endure all things.' The king was impressed.

**201** The king asked: 'How should a king conduct himself in public?' The scholar replied: 'With dignity and consistency, for his people look to him as a model.' The king was impressed.

**202** The king asked: 'What should a king do to maintain peace?' The scholar replied: 'Practice justice and show mercy, for these are the foundations of peace.' The king was impressed.

**295** When the translators arrived in Alexandria, the king gave them a magnificent welcome and set up a workplace for them on the island of Pharos.

**296** The island was fully equipped, and the translators worked in complete comfort and peace.

**297** They worked in groups, comparing their translations, and arrived at a perfect agreement among all seventy-two.

**298** The translation was finished in exactly seventy-two days — understood by all as a sign of divine providence.

**299** When the king heard that the work was done, he was overjoyed and praised the translators extravagantly.

**300** He read from the completed translation, and everyone who heard it was struck by its beauty and accuracy.

**301** The completed translation was presented before the assembled Jewish community of Alexandria.

**302** The priests, elders, and people gathered to hear the translation read aloud.

**303** When they heard it, they were deeply impressed and declared it to be an accurate and beautiful rendering of the Hebrew scriptures.

**304** They pronounced a curse on anyone who altered the translation in any way.

**305** 'This translation was produced under divine guidance,' they said. 'To change it would be to tamper with the word of God.'

**306** The king was overjoyed and ordered the translation placed in the royal library with the highest honor.

**307** He gave the translators magnificent gifts and let them return home to Jerusalem.

**308** Each of the seventy-two received three sets of fine clothes, two talents of gold, a golden cup, and a bed.

**309** They also received letters of commendation addressed to the High Priest Eleazar, praising their work.

**310** The king wrote to Eleazar: 'The work of your scholars has been enormously beneficial for this kingdom and for the whole world.'

**311** 'We have placed the translation in our royal library as the most honored book in the collection.'

**312** 'Please pray for us and for our kingdom.'

**313** Eleazar received the letter with great joy and gave thanks to God for inspiring the king.

**314** He replied: 'May the God of Israel bless and keep you, and may your kingdom prosper in peace.'

**315** And so the story of the translation of Moses' law into Greek comes to its conclusion.

**316** This is what I personally witnessed, Philocrates, and I have recorded it faithfully for you.

**317** I have neither exaggerated nor left out anything important, but told it as it actually happened.

**318** If you want to learn more about the Jewish law, you should read it yourself.

**319** In that law is contained all the wisdom anyone could need to live a good and righteous life.

**320** The God who gave the law is the God of all people, even though not everyone has come to know him yet.

**321** My prayer is that more and more people will come to know him and that his law will be honored by all nations.

**322** May God bless all who seek him sincerely. This is the end of the Letter of Aristeas to Philocrates.
